content: The World Health Organization (WHO) does not currently provide specific guidelines for managing needle-stick injuries. For participants with reactive initial test results, further testing can be conducted using venipuncture to collect additional blood samples for laboratory analysis. Dried blood spot (DBS) specimens are a practical method for transporting blood samples to laboratories, although the volume of blood collected is limited. To prevent cross-contamination, DBS samples must be carefully collected and handled. In the field, approximately 75 µL of capillary or venous blood (roughly one drop) is applied to filter paper using a precision pipette, and the spots are allowed to air dry. These samples are then individually packaged in bags with desiccants to maintain sample integrity during transport. DBS specimens are typically used with laboratory-based assays, and results are not returned to patients without confirmatory testing when used off-label. For venous blood sampling, specimens collected in serum separator tubes must be left at room temperature for at least 60 minutes to allow clot formation before being transported under refrigeration to the nearest laboratory. Specimens collected in EDTA tubes are transported refrigerated (2–8°C) and centrifuged at the laboratory. All specimens are transported in batches daily, and aliquots of serum are stored at 2–8°C if testing occurs within five days or at –20°C to –70°C for longer storage. Freezing and thawing cycles are avoided, and temperature monitoring is conducted throughout the process. Laboratory staff oversee specimen storage and processing upon arrival. For capillary blood sampling via finger-prick, the blood is either directly transferred to a test device or stored in micro-vials designed for capillary blood collection. DBS specimens are processed according to manufacturer or laboratory instructions, particularly in cases of off-label use. Testing strategies for hepatitis B virus (HBV) involve screening for HBsAg using either rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) or laboratory-based immunoassays. Reactive HBsAg results indicate HBV infection, while non-reactive results indicate no infection. WHO recommends a single serological assay for HBsAg detection, with confirmatory testing using neutralization steps or a second assay if necessary. For hepatitis C virus (HCV), testing begins with anti-HCV detection using RDTs or immunoassays. Reactive results are followed by supplementary testing for HCV RNA or core antigen to confirm current infection. WHO recommends RDTs in settings with limited laboratory access to improve linkage to care. For hepatitis A (HAV) and E (HEV), testing strategies are limited to detecting total antibodies or IgG antibodies. WHO does not currently have a standardized testing strategy for hepatitis D virus (HDV), leaving this to be defined by implementing teams. Specimen processing and data management follow strict quality assurance protocols, including daily checks for missing or inconsistent data, double data entry, and adherence to standard operating procedures (SOPs). Data cleaning and analysis are conducted prospectively, with anonymized databases and analysis scripts made available for review. Epidemiological data are analyzed to calculate crude prevalence and 95% confidence intervals, accounting for sampling weights and design effects. To minimize selection bias, field teams revisit households multiple times to reach selected participants. Community leaders are engaged to raise awareness and encourage participation. Recall bias is addressed by relying on vaccination cards or registries rather than participant memory. Interviewer bias is mitigated through standardized training and non-leading questioning techniques. Sample size calculations consider prevalence and design effects, with stratified analyses requiring careful interpretation due to potential imprecision. Serious adverse events are not expected, but any occurrences will be reported to the principal investigator within 24 hours. Participants diagnosed with HBV or HCV during the survey will be linked to care and treatment following WHO guidelines. Confidentiality is maintained through the use of unique identifier codes, and informed consent is obtained from all participants or their guardians. Children provide assent when appropriate, and all participants are informed of the risks and benefits of participation. Community engagement includes informing selected communities about the survey through local health officers and community leaders. Efforts are made to avoid stigmatization, emphasizing that viral hepatitis is not necessarily linked to high-risk behaviors.
